# Backpressure

Backpressure is the mechanism by which a slow downstream consumer signals an upstream producer to reduce its emission rate, rather than letting an unbounded buffer grow until the process runs out of memory.

## Implementation Patterns

The source describes three common approaches to implementing backpressure:

### Bounded Queues
The producer writes items to a queue with a fixed capacity. Once the queue is full, the producer blocks (or raises an error) until the consumer drains items, providing a natural synchronization point. This is a push-based model with built-in flow control.

### Credit-Based Flow Control
The consumer explicitly grants the producer permission to send N more items. The producer tracks available "credits" and only emits when it has remaining credit; the consumer replenishes credits as it processes items. This allows fine-grained control over how many items are in flight.

### Reactive-Pull Models
The consumer requests items on its own schedule rather than the producer pushing them. The producer does not emit until pulled, making the consumer the active driver of the data flow. This is pull-based control where the consumer naturally paces the pipeline.

## Context

Backpressure is essential in streaming pipelines where data arrival rates may exceed processing capacity. Without it, unbounded buffering leads to memory exhaustion and system instability. The choice of implementation depends on the architecture (push vs. pull), latency requirements, and throughput characteristics.
